title: Five LLM agents operate a browser from a plain-English goal, by reading the screen
hub: Five LLM agents operate a browser from a plain-English goal, by reading the screen
description: Pilot is a working prototype: five Gemini-powered agents that carry out a goal in a real browser by looking at screenshots, with a verifier that triggers replanning.
standfirst: Pilot types, clicks and scrolls in a real browser to carry out a goal such as "Move this lead to Proposal Sent", purely by looking at screenshots: no per-app API and no brittle page selectors. A verifier agent checks every step and sends a failed one back to the planner. It is a working prototype, and this page says plainly what it does not yet prove.

p: Can an agent operate any web app it can see, with no integration work for each one?

Five agents run as a loop. A screen interpreter turns a screenshot into structured UI state; a planner breaks the goal into steps; an action agent chooses a click, keystroke or scroll with pixel coordinates; a verifier looks at a fresh screenshot and either passes the step or triggers replanning; a narrator describes each step in the side panel.

It is built with a FastAPI backend (REST and WebSocket) and a Chrome Manifest V3 side-panel extension that dispatches real mouse and keyboard events through Chrome's debugger protocol. Each agent has its own prompt and returns JSON.

figure.caption: The agent loop, drawn from the code in backend/agents. A failed verification returns to the planner, up to three times per goal.

p: A code review on 2026-10-07 fixed three faults: replanning had no limit (it is now capped at [[3]] per goal), clicks on scaled displays landed at a multiple of the intended point (the extension now divides by the device pixel ratio), and a click outside the screenshot now fails the step instead of firing. [[11]] tests, with every model call stubbed, cover the loop.

limits: It is a prototype: session state is in memory, and the Terraform and Docker files are deployment scaffolding, not a verified live deployment.
There is no measured success rate. The repository holds a reliability model, but every rate in it is an assumption, not a measurement of Pilot.
That model suggests the verifier sets the ceiling: in a six-step base case, about one run in ten that Pilot reports as complete would be wrong, whatever the replan cap.
Every step costs a Gemini vision call, and reliability depends on the verifier catching mis-clicks.
